newsitem.title: USA: Witness tells of secondhand smoke risk in planes.
newsitem.headline: Witness tells of secondhand smoke risk in planes.

text.p: Flight attendants working in smoky aircraft cabins faced worse and riskier exposure to cancer-causing secondhand smoke than waiters and bartenders, a public health expert testified on Friday in a $5 billion anti-tobacco case.

Michael Siegel, a physician and expert on the causes of diseases, also told the jury that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer, emphysema and seven other diseases, as well as aggravating ailments such as respiratory disorders.
"I believe that secondhand smoke exposure in airline cabins caused lung cancer in flight attendants," said Siegel, a professor at the Boston University School of Public Health.

Siegel, whose testimony was repeatedly challenged by tobacco company lawyers, was called as a witness by lawyers pressing a landmark secondhand-smoke case on behalf of an estimated 60,000 non-smoking airline flight attendants with tobacco-related illnesses such as heart disease.
Other witnesses, including a former U.S. surgeon general, have also said since testimony began on Wednesday that secondhand smoke causes disease.

The tobacco companies fighting the lawsuit deny secondhand smoke is a health risk and say the average non-smoking flight attendant's exposure to secondhand smoke was trivial, before smoking was banned on U.S. airlines in 1988.

The author of a 1993 article in the Journal of the American Medical Association on secondhand-smoke risks among restaurant staff, Siegel said servers and bartenders spending eight-hour shifts in smokey places were much more heavily exposed to secondhand smoke than their customers and endured three to four times the exposure of a person sharing an office or a home with smokers.
Flight attendants working in enclosed cabins with no fresh air had even more secondhand-smoke exposure than food service workers, Siegel said.
Published measurements of secondhand smoke in airliner cabins were about twice the level found in restaurants, he said.

Smoking has been curbed or barred in many offices and public facilities throughout the United States since the mid-1980s, largely because of health worries about secondhand smoke, but is still largely allowed in bars and many restaurants.

Edward Moss, an attorney for Brown & Williamson Tobacco, one of the defendants, asked the trial judge to strike Siegel's testimony because a measurement for nicotine levels he gave for secondhand smoke during his testimony did not match the figure he gave during pre-trial questioning by tobacco company lawyers.

Judge Robert Kaye of Dade County Court refused. When questioned on the witness stand by Moss, Siegel said he had erred on the nicotine measurement during the questioning last May but had not altered his data.
The case, Norma Broin et al vs Philip Morris et al, is both the first secondhand-smoke case and the first class-action suit against the U.S. tobacco industry to come to trial. AMB.N
